questions.q: Which of these make a program easier to maintain? Tick all that apply.
options: Using variable names that say what the variable holds
Adding comments that explain why the code does what it does
Using single-letter names to keep the file short
correct: Using variable names that say what the variable holds
Adding comments that explain why the code does what it does
questions.feedback: Everything that makes code readable makes it maintainable. Short is not the same as clear.
questions.revisitLabel: 2.3 Lesson 3 — Code clinic, station 1: Naming conventions

questions.q: Explain why maintainability matters on a program that will be worked on for years.

markPoints.concept: the person maintaining it may not be the person who wrote it
accept: someone else|somebody else|another programmer|another person|different programmer|different person|new programmer|other people|team|not the author|not the original|not the person who wrote|did not write|not written by|original author|original programmer|original writer|rarely the
markPoints.exemplar: The person maintaining it is often not the person who wrote it.

markPoints.concept: so they have to understand it before they can change it safely
markPoints.exemplar: They have to understand it before they can change anything.

markPoints.concept: and unclear code takes longer to change and is easier to break
markPoints.exemplar: So unclear code takes longer to change and is much easier to break by accident.

questions.example: Over several years the person maintaining a program is usually not the person who wrote it, and quite often the author has forgotten it too. Whoever picks it up has to understand it before they can safely change anything, so code that is hard to follow takes much longer to work through and is far easier to break by accident.
questions.paraphrase: The programmer making changes later is rarely the original author, so they must first make sense of the code, and anything unclear slows that down because it raises the chance of introducing a fault.
questions.feedback: Three ideas: who, what they must do first, and the cost of it being hard.
questions.revisitLabel: 2.3 Lesson 3 — Code clinic, station 1: Naming conventions

questions.q: Which comment is the more useful in a maintainable program?
options: # VAT is applied before the discount, as required by the finance team
questions.feedback: A comment should say why, not restate what the line already says.
questions.revisitLabel: 2.3 Lesson 3 — Code clinic, station 1: Naming conventions

questions.q: Sort each habit by whether it is good practice or bad practice.
items: Indenting the body of every loop
Writing the whole program in one long block
Commenting why an unusual approach was taken
questions.feedback: Commenting every line is as unhelpful as commenting none: the useful comments get lost in the noise.
questions.revisitLabel: 2.3 Lesson 3 — Code clinic, station 1: Naming conventions

questions.q: Which variable name is the better choice in a maintainable program?
questions.feedback: A name that says what the variable holds saves the next reader working it out from how it is used.
questions.revisitLabel: 2.3 Lesson 3 — Code clinic, station 1: Naming conventions

questions.q: Explain how consistent indentation helps somebody reading a program.

markPoints.concept: it shows which lines are inside a loop or a condition
markPoints.exemplar: It shows which lines are inside a loop or an if statement.

markPoints.concept: so the structure can be seen without reading every line
accept: structure|shape|layout|see|seen|visible|obvious|glance|quickly|immediately|easier to follow|at a look|without reading|straight away
markPoints.exemplar: This means the structure of the program can be seen at a glance.

questions.example: Indentation shows which lines belong inside a loop or an if statement, so the shape of the program can be seen at a glance rather than worked out line by line. In Python it is not even optional — the indentation is what decides where a block ends.
questions.paraphrase: Because it makes clear which statements sit within a loop or condition, the layout of the program is visible immediately instead of having to be traced.
questions.feedback: What indentation shows, and what seeing it saves.
questions.revisitLabel: 2.3 Lesson 3 — Code clinic, station 1: Naming conventions

questions.q: In Python, indentation changes what a program does.
questions.feedback: In most languages indentation is only for readers. In Python it decides which lines are inside a block, so getting it wrong changes the program.
questions.revisitLabel: 2.3 Lesson 3 — Code clinic, station 1: Naming conventions

questions.q: Explain how breaking a program into sub-programs makes it easier to maintain.

markPoints.concept: each sub-program does one job and can be read on its own
accept: one job|one task|single task|one thing|single job|single purpose|own job|separately|on its own|by itself|smaller|short|self contained
markPoints.exemplar: Each sub-program does one job and can be read on its own.

markPoints.concept: so a change or a fix only has to be made in one place
accept: one place|once|single place|only there|reuse|reused|again|rest of the program|does not affect|without changing
markPoints.exemplar: This means a change only has to be made in one place rather than everywhere the code was repeated.

questions.example: Each sub-program does one job, so it can be read and understood without holding the whole program in your head. And because the code sits in one place rather than being copied, fixing it means changing one sub-program rather than hunting for every copy.
questions.paraphrase: Since every routine handles a single task it can be understood by itself, and as the code appears only once, a correction needs making in a single location.
questions.feedback: One job each, and the one place a fix goes.

questions.q: A program repeats the same eight lines in four different places. Put these steps in the order a programmer would take to improve it.
steps: Notice that the same eight lines appear four times
Work out what those eight lines do as one job
Write the eight lines once as a sub-program with a name that says that job
Replace each of the four copies with a call to the sub-program
Test that the program still behaves the same way
questions.feedback: Testing last is not optional: refactoring that is not tested is just editing.
